authoringScope: Unit 7 source-bound first-party teaching replacements only, excluding previously source-corrected lessons

lessons.title: Shapes That Are Solid
lessons.explanation: Sort and describe SOLID three-dimensional shapes using observable attributes. Students may invent their own sorting categories and explain them; do not require a single teacher-approved grouping.
lessons.examples: Example 1: A sphere rolls and has a curved surface. Example 2: A cube has six flat square faces. Example 3: A cylinder has two flat circular faces and one curved side.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Observe each object from several directions. Step 2: Choose a characteristic (flat faces, curved surfaces, rolling). Step 3: Group and explain the reason. Step 4: Check all members meet the stated rule.
lessons.mistakes: Do not treat a drawing of a circle as a physical sphere or require every shape to have corners.
lessons.summary: I can classify and describe solid shapes in my own accurate words.

lessons.title: Shapes That Are Flat
lessons.explanation: Sort FLAT two-dimensional shapes based on observable sides, curves and corners. Describe shapes in your own words before formal terminology.
lessons.examples: Example 1: A triangle is a closed flat shape with three straight sides. Example 2: A rectangle has four straight sides and four corners. Example 3: A circle has no straight sides or corners.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Examine each flat shape. Step 2: Count straight sides and corners, or notice curves. Step 3: Sort by the chosen shared feature. Step 4: Explain why each shape belongs.
lessons.mistakes: Do not confuse a 3D cube with its flat square face. A rotated triangle remains a triangle.
lessons.summary: I can sort and describe flat shapes using their attributes.

lessons.title: Some Triangles, All Triangles
lessons.explanation: Draw and identify triangles using DEFINING attributes rather than size, angle or orientation. A triangle is closed and has exactly three straight sides.
lessons.examples: Example 1: A small, tilted triangle is still a triangle because it has three connected straight sides. Example 2: Three separate sticks that do not form a closed boundary are not a triangle.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Draw three straight line segments. Step 2: Join their endpoints into one closed shape. Step 3: Count the three sides and vertices. Step 4: Change size or rotation and identify which features stay the same.
lessons.mistakes: Do not say a triangle must point up or have two matching sides. Rotation and color do not determine triangle membership.
lessons.summary: I can draw triangles and distinguish defining from non-defining features.

lessons.title: Equal Pieces
lessons.explanation: Determine whether a circle or rectangle is partitioned into EQUAL pieces and draw partitions into two or four equal shares.
lessons.examples: Example 1: A rectangle split down its middle into two equal rectangles has halves. Example 2: A circle split through its center by two perpendicular diameters has four equal fourths. Unequal pieces are not halves.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Identify the complete circle or rectangle. Step 2: Divide into two equal areas for halves. Step 3: Divide into four equal areas for fourths. Step 4: Compare the piece sizes and name the equal shares.
lessons.mistakes: Do not call any two pieces halves: they must have equal area. Different-looking pieces must be checked rather than assumed equal.
lessons.summary: I can partition circles and rectangles into halves and fourths.

lessons.title: One of the Pieces, All of the Pieces
lessons.explanation: Describe how two halves or four fourths make one complete shape, and name ONE equal piece as a half or fourth of that whole.
lessons.examples: Example 1: Two equal halves of a rectangle make one whole. Example 2: Four equal fourths of a circle make one whole. Example 3: One of four equal squares in a partitioned rectangle is one fourth of the rectangle.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Show the whole. Step 2: Verify pieces are equal in area. Step 3: Count two equal halves or four equal fourths. Step 4: Identify one piece using a correct part-of-whole description.
lessons.mistakes: Do not call one of three unequal pieces a fourth. Names halves and fourths depend on the total number of equal pieces.
lessons.summary: I can describe a whole and its equal halves or fourths.

lessons.title: A Bigger Piece PLC Activity
lessons.explanation: Compare halves and fourths of the SAME original shape. Partitioning one whole into more equal shares makes each share smaller.
lessons.examples: Example 1: One half of the same rectangle is larger in area than one fourth. Example 2: Two fourths cover the same area as one half of the same whole.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Draw one rectangle and two identical copies. Step 2: Split one into two equal halves and another into four equal fourths. Step 3: Compare a single piece in each. Step 4: Explain that more equal pieces means smaller individual pieces.
lessons.mistakes: Do not compare one fourth of a big shape to one half of a much smaller shape and claim a universal ordering.
lessons.summary: I can explain why fourths are smaller than halves of the same whole.

lessons.title: Center Day 2
lessons.explanation: Teacher-led shape center review: compose objects from solids, describe shapes in picture books, add within 100 and subtract within 10. Digital arithmetic cannot certify building or explaining an object.
lessons.examples: Example 1: A cube and rectangular prism can be arranged into a new solid structure. Example 2: 47+28=75 by combining tens and ones. Example 3: 9-4=5.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Identify the selected activity's exact goal. Step 2: For shapes, describe and build with appropriate solids. Step 3: For mathematics, use a suitable addition or subtraction method. Step 4: Explain the result to the teacher.
lessons.mistakes: Do not replace a three-dimensional composition with an unrelated arithmetic question and claim the shape objective was assessed.
lessons.summary: I can work accurately with solids, addition within 100 and subtraction within 10 in their respective centers.

lessons.title: Center Day 3
lessons.explanation: Teacher-led center review: add within 100, name and describe two- and three-dimensional shapes, or subtract within 10. Each center has a different mathematical goal.
lessons.examples: Example 1: 35+46=81. Example 2: 8-3=5. Example 3: A flat triangle has three straight sides; a three-dimensional cone has a circular base and curved surface.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Read the center's task and expected representation. Step 2: Use place-value addition, small subtraction or shape attributes as appropriate. Step 3: Check and explain your result. Step 4: Teacher validates hands-on shape activity and partner work.
lessons.mistakes: Do not claim the hands-on shape activity is complete merely because one number was entered digitally.
lessons.summary: I can choose correct calculation and shape language in teacher-led centers.
